entries.title: Hybrid Plasmon-Phonon Eigenmodes and Vortex States in a Graphene Ring on a Silica Substrate
entries.abstract: We investigate hybrid plasmon-phonon eigenmodes and localized electromagnetic vortex states in a graphene ring supported by a dispersive silica substrate. The interaction between graphene plasmons and infrared-active optical phonons of the substrate gives rise to distinct spectral branches of surface polaritons, whose dispersion characteristics are established analytically and validated by full-wave numerical simulations. Geometric confinement of these hybrid surface excitations produces spectrally separated families of localized multipolar eigenmodes with corresponding azimuthal symmetries. Particular attention is devoted to quadrupolar eigenstates, which exhibit nearly identical normalized spatial field distributions despite their substantial spectral separation and different attenuation characteristics. We demonstrate that coherent superposition of orthogonal quadrupolar field patterns gives rise to localized vortex states with opposite azimuthal phase winding. The preservation of the spatial eigenmode structure across distinct spectral branches is consistent with a quasistatic description in which the resonator geometry governs the modal symmetry, whereas the dispersive material response determines the spectral properties. These findings reveal a route toward controlling structured electromagnetic near fields through plasmon–phonon hybridization and establish a physical basis for multiband vortex states in deeply subwavelength graphene resonators.

entries.title: Photonic processors that carry their own unclonable fingerprint
entries.abstract: Physically unclonable functions (PUFs) derive cryptographic keys from uncontrollable fabrication disorder, removing the need to store secrets in vulnerable non-volatile memory. Programmable photonic processors are natural candidates for PUFs, because each of their many tunable interferometers carries its own fabrication imperfections. However, we show that the mesh topology itself funnels light along short paths, so that most of this disorder contributes little to the response. Here we introduce an isotropic ring routing scheme that steers light to the core of a hexagonal mesh and redistributes it uniformly towards the perimeter, suppressing a distance-dependent power decay of 14.7 dB and raising the mean Shannon entropy of the response from 1.95 to 3.48 bits by reprogramming alone. Experiments on two independently fabricated 72-unit silicon processors show that a nominally identical device cannot reproduce the target's responses even after its passive phase profile is fully compensated. Combining isotropic routing with spectral readout yields 1107 bits per challenge, exceeding previous results by two orders of magnitude, with 49.8% inter-challenge and 50.0% inter-chip Hamming distances and a 4.9% intra-chip distance. These results establish general-purpose programmable photonic processors as reconfigurable, high-capacity hardware roots of trust.
entries.comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Includes Supplementary Information

entries.title: Exceptional unidirectional radiation modes
entries.abstract: Singularities such as exceptional points (EPs) and bound states in the continuum (BICs) fundamentally reshape the spectral response of non-Hermitian open systems, unlocking exotic physical phenomena and unprecedented ways of wave manipulation. Nevertheless, the radiation behaviors of modes evolving around these singularities lack a unified picture. Here we show that a mode originating from a BIC can radiate unidirectionally, exhibiting a quality factor that continuously varies in parameter space from a near-infinite value (near the BIC) to a finite lower bound as it coalesces with the other (leaky) mode at an EP. The crossing of the unidirectional radiation mode and the EP in parameter space results in not only merged poles (resonant EP) but also merged zeros (absorbing EP) of the scattering matrix, along with a counterintuitive reversal of radiation direction decoupled from the coalesced eigenmodes under near-field excitation. These phenomena are experimentally observed in an acoustic waveguide system featuring two side-branch resonant cavities with deliberate frequency detuning and asymmetric dissipation. Our findings reveal the intrinsic connection between eigenmode topology and radiation behavior in open systems, offering a viable route for tailoring scattering and radiation responses via non-Hermitian modulations.

entries.title: A Symmetry-Stratified Framework for Phase Transitions: Thermodynamic States, Critical Dynamics, and Spectral Mechanical Signatures
entries.abstract: Structural symmetry, thermodynamic phase stability, and elastic-wave response provide related but distinct descriptions of a transforming solid. We formulate a symmetry-stratified framework that connects these descriptions through a finite-dimensional internal state and a parent-invariant free energy. Stabilizers classify structural states, whereas free-energy comparisons and stability conditions determine equilibrium branches and dissipative evolution. Equivariance ensures that the frozen elastic tangent inherits the structural stabilizer. Equality requires additional identifiability conditions. Little-group representations and degenerate perturbation theory then determine whether an acoustic doublet splits and the first nonzero splitting order p. On a selected continuous branch with order-parameter exponent β, a regular, observable acoustic gap scales as |t|^(pβ), provided critical self-energies and structural relaxation do not dominate the measurement. Explicit tensorial and cubic-to-tetragonal realizations yield linear and quadratic splitting channels, together with directionally protected degeneracies. Separate numerical benchmarks examine free-energy reconstruction, coexistence, elastic compatibility, finite-temperature spectra, and controlled critical readouts. Reanalysis of NiTi measurements illustrates effective elastic degeneracy, thermal-history dependence, and the predictive value of independently measured phase fractions. Most importantly, the framework identifies the constitutive and measurement assumptions required to infer structural changes from mechanical spectra.

entries.title: Geometric control of diffusive relaxation: spectral design, transport bounds and transverse mode isolation
entries.abstract: Geometric confinement changes both thermal relaxation and heat throughput, but these effects need not be governed by the same conduction path. We establish a distinction between serial and parallel geometries for passive, homogeneous Fourier conductors at fixed material properties, volume and length. For a reduced variable-area conductor, two logarithmic shape harmonics independently tune two selected Bloch-rate pairs, and exact local transport level sets permit spectral redistribution at fixed effective diffusivity. A nonperturbative weighted Poincaré bound, however, requires the effective axial diffusivity to vanish if the first positive insulated rate tends to zero at fixed length. This obstruction is avoided by continuous parallel paths with weak transverse exchange. Capacity-weighted networks identify the exchange mechanism, and a three-dimensional product domain provides an exact bulk realization. Its axial conductance remains κV/L², while exactly one positive insulated rate vanishes and the next approaches a positive limit set by axial, chamber and neck diffusion. The slow rate is asymptotically the transverse neck conductance times the sum of inverse chamber capacities. Spectral projection estimates translate this separation into a preparation- and readout-dependent observation window. The result is metastable retention of a temperature contrast under insulated conditions, not a second equilibrium state. It identifies when geometrical control of internal equilibration can be separated from macroscopic heat transport.

entries.title: Colloquium: Isotopes for medicine and fundamental physics
entries.abstract: Isotopes, variants of elements distinguished by their neutron number, have important applications for medicine and fundamental science. This review explores the historical challenges and new technologies for enriching and detecting isotopes. We motivate the work by challenges posed by three of history's greatest scientists: James Clerk Maxwell's thought experiment on thermodynamics, Ernest Rutherford's practical dilemma in radiochemistry, and Albert Einstein's questions about the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. The journey to meet these challenges has catalyzed the development of innovative techniques for isotope separation. These advancements can mitigate the worldwide crisis in the supply of enriched isotopes. We then explore the expected impact of these new technologies on medicine, which include radioisotopes for cancer therapy and stable isotopes as tracers for metabolism. We explain the importance of developing scalable techniques for isotope detection and how it can help with early detection of certain diseases. Finally, we turn to basic science, outlining proposed new tests of quantum mechanics that utilize radioactive atomic clocks to probe the fundamental nature of determinism and distinguishability of atoms.

entries.title: Design and Modeling of Graded Base III-Nitride HBTs for High-Frequency Applications
entries.abstract: This work analyzes the high-frequency performance constraints of AlGaN/GaN heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) and proposes a novel band-engineered graded base N-polar AlGaN/GaN HBT and evaluates the RF performances. Unlike conventional p-GaN base designs, we propose a graded base in the N-polar orientation which offers polarization-induced hole accumulation with quasi-electric field-assisted minority carrier transport. The proposed design simultaneously mitigates the longstanding current crowding, Webster effect, and conventional base resistance limitations. Using well-calibrated two-dimensional TCAD simulations, the proposed compositionally graded base HBT projects peak f_T/f_MAX of 190/200 GHz with a power density (V_BRI_MAX/8 > 20 W/mm), offering a promising pathway toward simultaneous high-frequency and high-power GaN millimeter-wave electronics.

entries.title: Generation of neutron Bessel beams
entries.abstract: Matter waves can exhibit structured wavefields analogous to those of light, offering new means of controlling the spatial and angular-momentum degrees of freedom of massive particles. Bessel beams are a fundamental class of structured waves that exhibit non-diffracting propagation, self-healing, and well-defined orbital angular momentum (OAM). Here, we experimentally realize neutron Bessel beams by imprinting a nanoscale conical phase gradient onto a neutron wavefront. By incorporating azimuthal phase gradients, we generate zeroth-, third-, and sixth-order Bessel beams, demonstrating direct control of both the OAM and radial structure of a massive particle. We also propose a neutron Bessel-grating interferometer, complementary to established optical and electron interferometric methods, in which varying the radial grating period by approximately 100 nm yields a controlled Gouy phase shift of π. These results establish neutron Bessel beams as a new platform for diffractive neutron focusing and provide an experimental foundation for theoretical studies of Bessel beams in neutron scattering, decay, and OAM characterization.

entries.title: Reliable arithmetic circuits using less reliable (sub-digital) logic
entries.abstract: The frequent static failure of CMOS logic gates at ultra-low voltages has historically been perceived as a strict barrier to extreme voltage scaling: this paper introduces a statistical circuit law proving this intuition wrong. We discovered a universal power law connecting gate and circuit static failure probabilities, revealing that circuit failure requires the simultaneous breakdown of an entire gate cluster rather than a single component. Because the required cluster size increases rapidly as voltage drops, low-voltage sub-digital logic exhibits surprising inherent resilience to static failure. This insight stems from new theoretical tools we developed to quantify static failure, extending well beyond conventional voltage-margin analysis. Consequently, sub-digital processors could potentially offer a viable, near-term solution to drastically reduce the energy demands of AI.

entries.title: Mid-Infrared Integrated Acousto-Optic Phase Modulation on GaAs/AlGaAs
entries.abstract: We demonstrate a mid-infrared (7.5-10 um) integrated acousto-optic phase modulator operating at 460MHz based on a GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure. The combination of broad mid-infrared transparency and piezoelectric properties of GaAs based structures allows monolithic integration of all the device functions (electro-acoustic transduction and acousto-optic interaction) on a single material platform. Addressing the challenge presented by comparable mid-infrared and acoustic wavelengths, simultaneous propagation and confinement of surface acoustic waves and guided light is achieved using a deep-etched sub-wavelength grating. We develop a comprehensive and quantitative simulation framework to design the modulator devices, characterize their acoustic properties in a heterodyne vibrometer and perform a full, quantitative analysis of the device performance by inserting them in an integrated Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Remarkable agreement with simulations validates the proposed design flow, and opens the way to improved integrated acousto-optic devices operating in the longer end of the mid-infrared.

entries.title: Nonideal Absorbers in Hot-Carrier and Hot-Absorber Solar Cells: Losses and Heat Recycling
entries.abstract: The hot carrier solar cell exhibits a photovoltaic conversion efficiency limit of 85.4%. Among the idealizations necessary to achieve this efficiency, it has traditionally been considered essential that the electrons absorbing sunlight do not end up transferring the captured energy to the crystal lattice. In this work, we argue that such a requirement is not necessary if the absorber is thermally insulated. In our analysis, we also consider the possibility of ohmic losses in the absorber due to finite electrical conductivity. We also demonstrate that such losses, delivered as heat, can be partially recycled into electrical work with an efficiency that is given by the Carnot factor. The high efficiencies reported here are thermodynamic limits obtained with ideal energy-selective contacts and negligible parasitic contact conductance, not projections of practical device efficiency. Our work includes a sensitivity analysis for finite contact-mediated heat leakage, and the results are presented as design targets.
entries.journalRef: Ines Duran, Simon Svatek, Irene Artacho, Elisa Antolin, and Antonio Marti. Nonideal Absorbers in Hot-Carrier and Hot-Absorber Solar Cells: Losses and Heat Recycling. Physical Review Applied 26, no. 3 (2026): 034049

entries.title: Observation of room-temperature intrinsic antiferroelectricity in van der Waals NbOCl2
entries.abstract: In recent years, two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectricity has been extensively investigated across a wide range of 2D materials, while intrinsic 2D antiferroelectricity remains exceptionally rare, limiting its implementation in next-generation photonic and electronic devices. Here, we report the observation of room-temperature-stable antiferroelectricity in the layered transition metal oxyhalide NbOCl2, and demonstrate a reversible, stimuli-driven antiferroelectric-to-ferroelectric (AFE-to-FE) phase transition in this material. Second-harmonic generation (SHG) mapping reveals a well-defined stripe-like spatial distribution of SHG intensity across as-grown NbOCl2 flakes spanning thickness from few-layer to bulk-like configurations. This distinctive SHG signature originates from the existence of antiferroelectric phase and the coexistence of antiferroelectric and ferroelectric phases within individual crystals, as evidenced by a combined incident-angle-dependent SHG measurement and Raman spectroscopy. By integrating NbOCl2 with one-dimensional silver nanowires, we achieve spatially selective, strain-mediated AFE-to-FE phase transition. Moreover, an ultralow electric field (20 kV/cm) induces a reversible SHG response, consistent with switching from the centrosymmetric antiferroelectric state (SHG-silent) to the non-centrosymmetric ferroelectric state (SHG-active). This study not only expands the family of room-temperature 2D antiferroelectrics but also establishes a versatile platform for dynamic manipulation of nonlinear light, paving the way toward electric-field-programmable nonlinear photonics and optical information processing.

entries.title: Optical Neural Networks Should Be Evaluated by Function, Not Only Physics
entries.abstract: Optical neural networks (ONNs) are attracting significant attention as alternative platforms for machine learning (ML). In an ONN, an optical module often takes over part of the computation inside a digital ML pipeline. How much of the task does the optical module itself perform, and how much does it contribute to any claimed system-level advantages, such as throughput or energy? This paper offers a simple, function-oriented evaluation methodology. Whatever its internal physics, the optical module appears to the surrounding digital pipeline as a mapping between real-valued tensors. We therefore evaluate it in three steps: (i) define its boundary in the pipeline, as real-valued tensors in and out; (ii) replace it with standard digital modules to identify those that match the optical system's performance on the same task and metric; and (iii) state system-level claims, such as speed or energy, per inference against the performance-matched digital module. We summarize steps (i) and (ii) in an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its use on published ONN systems. This helps isolate the optical module's contribution and provides a concrete digital reference for assessing its claimed system-level advantages, without the need to understand the physics. While we focus on optical systems as the most prominent example, the same approach applies to any physical analog computing platform used in ML, wherever a physical module takes over part of a digital pipeline.

entries.title: Quantum amplification with a linear quantum coupler
entries.abstract: Josephson parametric amplifiers (JPAs) are essential components for quantum-limited microwave measurement, but their dynamic range is often constrained by Kerr and other pump-induced nonlinear effects. In this work, we systematically study the performance of a parametric amplifier based on the linear inductive coupler (LINC). Starting from the driven-circuit Hamiltonian, we derive the effective three-wave-mixing amplifier model, including leading flux-driven nonlinear corrections relevant to realistic operation. We analyze the resulting gain response, saturation behavior, and intermodulation distortion, comparing them with representative state-of-the-art JPA designs. Our results show that the symmetry-protected structure of the LINC suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity. Moreover, suitable circuit-parameter optimization can further reduce the dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects, leading to considerable improvements in power-handling metrics. These results identify the LINC architecture as a promising platform for high-linearity Josephson parametric amplification.

entries.title: Temperature Flips the Sign of the Hydrogen Response in Nanogranular Palladium Networks
entries.abstract: In nanogranular palladium networks, hydrogen uptake has two opposing effects on electrical resistance. Absorbed hydrogen scatters electrons within the particles, raising their resistance, while particle expansion narrows the gaps between them and lowers the junction resistance. Such networks are widely studied as resistive hydrogen sensors, and the sign of their net response is usually treated as a fixed property of the architecture. In networks grown by atomic layer deposition on macroporous silicon, we show that changing the operating temperature can reverse this sign at a fixed hydrogen concentration. A thermodynamic model indicates that scattering contributes less as temperature rises, allowing sub-angstroem changes in gap width to dominate. Where the two effects cancel, the network absorbs hydrogen yet gives the same reading as in hydrogen-free gas, so a leak could escape detection. Between 25 and 40 degrees Celsius, this cancellation point is predicted to rise over tenfold, crossing reported leak-alarm setpoints. At 55 degrees Celsius, the measured response stays negative but passes through a minimum, so a concentration above a setpoint can mimic one below it. Annealing at 200 degrees Celsius alters the calibration and turns the room-temperature response negative at the lowest concentration tested. Quantitative sensing therefore requires a defined thermal pretreatment and an operating temperature giving distinct signals across the intended concentration range. Response polarity becomes an operating parameter rather than a fixed property. More broadly, any nanoparticle network whose particles deform on sorption may show the same temperature-dependent competition between transport within and between particles, with implications for sensors and switches beyond palladium-hydrogen.

entries.title: Thermal and Acoustic Measurements of Hybrid Bonding Stacks
entries.abstract: Thermal and structural characterizations of hybrid bonding structures are essential for understanding heat transport in three-dimensional integrated circuits (3D-ICs). In this work, we investigate the effective thermal conductivity of the Cu/dielectric HB layer using time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) combined with picosecond ultrasonic technique. Shallow-angle polishing enabled depth-resolved thermal measurements by exposing hybrid bonding layers with different remaining thicknesses, while acoustic echoes were used to identify buried interfaces and determine the thickness. The distinct waveform of the bonding interface echo compared with the Cu/dielectric interface echo suggests that its acoustic response may also reflect the interfacial bonding conditions. The extracted thermal conductivity ranges from 1.14 to 1.75 Wm-1K-1 for the bottom pad layer and from 1.76 to 4.34 Wm-1K-1 for the top pad layer. The difference in thermal conductivity is consistent with the different Cu area fractions of the two layers. Furthermore, the thermal conductivity of the top pad layer increases significantly with the remaining thickness, possibly due to the thermal boundary resistance at the bonding interface, low thermal conductivity of SiCN interlayer, and increased electron scattering in thin Cu structures. Our work demonstrates a practical approach to investigate the thermal properties of buried hybrid bonding layers, providing experimental data for thermal design and modeling of 3D-ICs.

entries.title: Development and Validation of a preCICE Based OpenMOC OpenFOAM Coupling Framework for Nuclear Reactor Analysis
entries.abstract: To address the long computation time required by stochastic solvers, which are applied in the coupled neutronics-thermal hydraulics (N-TH) calculations, a faster N-TH coupling framework is developed based on the multiphysics coupling library preCICE, which enables data exchange between OpenMOC and OpenFOAM. As an alternative to commonly used stochastic solvers, like OpenMC, OpenMOC is used as a neutronics solver providing much faster steady-state solution in a Picard iteration. To realize this coupling strategy, OpenMC is used for an initial one-time computation cost for multi-group cross sections data generation that is used throughout OpenMOC calculations. A preCICE library adapter for OpenMOC is also developed, allowing data exchange between neutronic power distributions and thermal hydraulic temperature fields. Our proposed coupling framework is validated through simulations of a simplified 2 times 2 fuel assembly, and a quartered geometry of 17 times 17 fuel assembly. The comparison shows good agreement with established referenced solutions, highlighting our proposed coupling framework for the steady-state N-TH coupling at a fraction of the time required by stochastic solver codes. This advantages could be extended for future applications where fast approximated solutions are required to address the change of N-TH coupling due to small parametric changes like in digital twin of nuclear reactor.

entries.title: Swift Heavy Ion Tracks in Polymorphs of Titanium Dioxide: The Effects of Electron Beam and Crystal Structures
entries.abstract: Swift heavy ion (SHI) irradiation generates nanoscale damage in materials, offering opportunities for controlled modification of structural properties. Understanding the fundamental processes governing damage formation in altered regions remains a longstanding challenge. This work explores how crystal structure influences swift heavy ion-induced damage formation and evolution in rutile and anatase TiO2. Combining transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate how differences in atomic arrangement govern track morphology and structural recovery. Although irradiation produces amorphous tracks in both polymorphs, their morphologies differ considerably. In rutile, tracks develop pronounced diameter variations, forming hourglass-like structures, whereas in anatase they retain a relatively uniform cylindrical shape. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that these differences arise from the distinct recrystallization behavior of the two crystal structures during rapid cooling, leading to different pathways of track evolution and recovery. Particular attention is paid to electron beam induced effects during TEM characterization, which can substantially modify the structure and apparent morphology of ion tracks. Prolonged electron beam exposure promotes the recrystallization of initially amorphous tracks and surface hillocks, accompanied by the development of Fresnel contrast. These findings highlight the importance of understanding beam-induced transformations for the reliable interpretation of TEM observations of radiation-damaged materials.

entries.title: Second Harmonic Flexoelectricity
entries.abstract: Flexoelectricity (polarization induced by strain gradients) is assumed to be insensitive to space inversion in all materials: flexoelectric polarization should not depend on whether a crystal is bent upwards or downwards. In this work, we show that this assumption is wrong for ferroelectrics of all thickness and at all curvatures, owing to an intrinsic quadratic contribution that persists down to strain gradients of 1 m-1 or less, which is millions of times smaller than conventional expectations for nonlinear flexoelectricity. As a consequence, ferroelectric crystals can generate second-harmonic voltage at twice the oscillation frequency of the bending.

entries.title: QCap: a physics-corrected graph neural network for the capacitance matrix of any planar superconducting device layout
entries.abstract: Electromagnetic simulations of device layouts to extract capacitance are computationally intensive, a major obstacle to accurate design of circuit devices. Machine learning models can bypass these simulations, but previous approaches have been restricted to layouts using only particular components, and require thousands of simulations of those same components as training data. We present QCap, a model that accurately predicts the Maxwell capacitance matrix of an arbitrary superconducting device layout in seconds, compared to minutes to hours of Ansys Q3D simulations. We develop a novel design-embedding algorithm that converts the layout into a universal graph format, allowing the model to work with any layout created with any tool. To achieve high accuracy, we obtain a coarse physics prior from a fast method of moments simulation of capacitance, then train the model to correct this prior. On 4,009 test designs withheld from training data the model outputs agree with Q3D simulations to a median error of 0.177%, and on never-seen component families it stays below 1% error. We demonstrate the model's scaling by obtaining the capacitance matrix of a 9-superconducting-qubit device in 12 seconds on a laptop (compared to 19.9 h and 228 GB of memory in Ansys) with sub-percent error, and capacitance of a (too large to simulate) 100-qubit, 781-conductor device in 3.4 min on a laptop. We provide the open-source models and data on SQuADDS and Hugging Face. Our results provide a powerful tool for large-scale accurate circuit design and guide the development of models to bypass other physical simulations.
entries.comment: 26 pages, 13 figures, 8 tables. Models, data and tutorials: https://lfl-lab.github.io/SQuADDS/qcap/

entries.title: Bandwidth-tunable thermal emitter via dynamic resonator coupling and loss
entries.abstract: We demonstrate a dynamically tunable omnidirectional thermal emitter that can be switched from a narrowband emission state to a broadband state. The structure is a metal-backed multilayer with subwavelength thickness across the mid-infrared, which forms an angle-insensitive (up to 60°) optical cavity with one input port. We used an ultrathin VO2 layer to dynamically switch the coupling and loss coefficients of this optical cavity, resulting in narrowband emission from the vibrational mode of a polar dielectric layer that is part of the multilayer stack when the VO2 is in its insulating phase, and broadband emission from a nearly impedance-matched cavity when the VO2 is switched to its lossy metallic phase. We fabricated the structure around a free-standing silicon membrane and integrated it onto a printed circuit board (PCB), which enabled electrical switching of the emitter at the ten-to-hundred millisecond scale, and can be used for free-space identification, tagging, or communication.

entries.title: Spatiotemporal programming of shape memory polymers for tunable vibration responses
entries.abstract: Stimuli-responsive materials offer a promising route to dynamically tailor material behavior, enabling adaptive functionalities in changing environments. However, simultaneously implementing spatial and temporal control in active material systems remains a fundamental challenge. Here, we present a photothermally programmable shape memory polymer (SMP) metamaterial platform that enables dynamic control of elastic wave propagation through reconfigurable spatiotemporal temperature distributions. By projecting user-defined light patterns onto carbon-doped SMP (C-SMP) surfaces, spatial thermomechanical property landscapes are generated, enabling a wide range of elastic wave functionalities, including tunable transmission spectra and programmable vibrational modes. By treating both space and time as design parameters, we access an expanded design space that allows a bulk C-SMP surface to function as a highly adaptive metamaterial platform. This work establishes spatiotemporal property modulation as a powerful framework for adaptive vibration control, tunable phononic systems, and other advanced dynamic applications.

entries.title: Radiation Response of NbN Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detectors Under ²¹⁰Po Alpha-Particle Irradiation
entries.abstract: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) are attractive for space applications because they combine high detection efficiency, low noise, and fast timing, but their radiation tolerance remains less established than that of conventional semiconductor detectors. Here we study NbN SNSPDs exposed to alpha-particle ²¹⁰Po irradiation by combining cryogenic electrical and photon-counting measurements with SRIM and Geant4 radiation-transport calculations. For the estimated fluence corresponding to the 200-hour ²¹⁰Po exposure, the air-inclusive Geant4 calculation predicts an average ionizing dose of 8.49 Mrad in the active NbN layer and a displacement-damage estimate of 5.67 ×10⁻⁷ displacements per atom. Measurements before and after irradiation show no systematic degradation of the superconducting transition, switching current, retrapping current, dark-count behavior, or photon-count response. These results indicate radiation resilience of thin-film NbN SNSPDs under a multi-Mrad alpha-particle exposure and support their use in photon-counting systems for radiation environments.

entries.title: Surrogate-Assisted Compact-Model Extraction for SKY130 CMOS at 77 K
entries.abstract: Cryogenic circuit design requires compact transistor models that reproduce measured low-temperature behavior and run in standard circuit simulators. We fit BSIM4 parameters to measured I-V curves of SkyWater 130 nm (SKY130) transistors at 77 K using a neural surrogate of NGSpice. The surrogate maps compact-model parameters and device geometry to the complete set of output and transfer characteristics. Extraction is a bounded least-squares search: a bank of NGSpice simulations supplies initial candidates, finite differences of the surrogate supply the local Jacobian, and NGSpice re-simulates the resulting cards before selection. On 18 measured geometries, we compare a search over seven card parameters with a search over 43 parameters selected by NGSpice sensitivity. Relative to NGSpice re-simulations of the previously released cards, the two searches reduce the in-sample mean relative root-mean-square error (RRMS) by 17% and 26%, respectively. The 43-parameter search has the lower overall error, but the seven-parameter search has the lower mean on high-bias curves, and some individual curves have higher error than with the released cards under both searches.

entries.title: Shared-State Inverse Synthesis of Dual-Mode Conformal Metasurfaces for Low Scattering and Telemetry
entries.abstract: A conformal surface that alternates between sectoral low scattering and directive telemetry poses a shared-hardware inverse problem when both modes must use one finite passive impedance alphabet, although their spatial codebooks may differ. This paper formulates and solves that mixed continuous–discrete problem at the effective impedance-boundary level. Reference-centered Tikhonov preimages prescribe restricted radiation data; inverse-source null-space freedom then moves each current within its data-equivalent class toward impedance profiles quantizable by the same alphabet. A line-searched Gauss–Newton update, common-state assignment and projected-centroid updates, and exact forward refinement determine the currents, two codebooks, and one passive library. Data invariance, the current-to-impedance differential, the optimal state update, monotonic mismatch reduction, and a forward perturbation bound are derived. A full-mutual-coupling two-dimensional TM study of a 4λ₀-diameter cylinder uses 64 physical cells and one shared eight-state library. On a 256-unknown validation model, the worst power ratio over ±10° monostatic sectors and incidence angles from -30° to 30° is -11.6 dB relative to a PEC cylinder; telemetry directivity is 13.1 dB with -13.6-dB peak sidelobes and a 1° pointing error. A separate Fourier–Galerkin formulation, converged through 513 complex modes without reoptimization, gives -11.36 dB and 13.02 dB for the corresponding worst-sector and directivity metrics. The results establish feasibility at the effective impedance-boundary level; they do not establish unit-cell, bias-network, or platform-level realizability.

entries.title: Multilevel AlScN Ferroelectric Diode Crossbar Arrays with Sub-200 nm Cells for Selector-Free Nonvolatile Memory
entries.abstract: Passive crossbar arrays are a leading route to high-density nonvolatile memory and in-memory computing, but without a selector the memory element itself must supply the nonlinearity that suppresses sneak-path currents. Here we scale aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN) ferroelectric diodes (FeDs) in both dimensions that matter - the ferroelectric is thinned to 10 nm and the junction diameter is reduced to 100 nm. We further integrate 200 nm cells into a 2-kilobyte (128 * 128) passive crossbar. At a junction area of 0.0314 um2 this is a ~625 reduction in cell area, at equal array capacity, relative to kilobyte-scale AlScN FeD crossbars built on 5 μm cells. The 10 nm Al0.64Sc0.36N layer reverses its polarization under pulses of 50 ns full width at half maximum at a pulse-energy density of ~16 pJ μm-2, corresponding to ~0.5 pJ per 200 nm cell. Pulsed programming at 17.5 V and 1 kHz yields an ON/OFF ratio of 4.2 * 103 in a 200 nm cell, while DC characterization of 283 randomly addressed cells of the 2-kB array gives ON/OFF and rectification ratios at 5 V of 43 33 and 61 74, from which we derive the sub-array size that selector-free reading currently supports. Eight conductance levels (three bits) written into a 200 nm array cell remain resolvable for 103 s, and the two extreme states are stable beyond 5 * 104 s. Mapping the measured, nonuniformly spaced levels onto a ResNet-20 network recovers 91.7 +- 0.1% CIFAR-10 accuracy after quantization-aware training, against a 92.2 +- 0.1% full-precision baseline. AlScN FeDs thus combine nanosecond switching, three-bit storage and sub-0.05 μm2 cells in a BEOL-compatible, selector-free crossbar.

entries.title: Immersive virtual reality in learning physics: a systematic review of opportunities and challenges
entries.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) can heighten presence and enable active, embodied interaction in realistic 3D environments, which has been associated with potential benefits in physics education. This article presents a comprehensive review of IVR implementation in physics education at both school and university levels. The analysis included 34 studies indexed in Scopus and ERIC, published between 1 January 2018 and 1 June 2025. Methodologically, this review followed a preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses approach. IVR implementations for physics learning were assessed, topic-aligned activity types were summarized, and associated opportunities and challenges were documented. Findings indicate that IVR can support physics learning by providing complementary visualizations, optimizing cognitive load, enabling haptic learning, saving time, and fostering collaborative inquiry. Conversely, the most frequent potential IVR challenges include discomfort, unreliable interaction, orchestration issues, relatively high costs, and significant extraneous cognitive load.

entries.title: Laser Processing for Energy Applications
entries.abstract: Laser processing has emerged as a transformative technology in the energy sector, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable solutions for energy generation, storage, and sustainability. This chapter explores the diverse applications of laser technology in energy applications. It begins with an overview of laser-driven inertial confinement fusion for energy production, highlighting key experimental facilities and crucial laser parameters. The role of lasers in solar energy harvesting is examined, including photovoltaic cell optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted recycling of solar modules. The chapter further reviews recent developments into laser-based techniques for enhancing electrochemical performance through surface texturing at various scales. Advancements in lithium-ion battery technology are also discussed, focusing on next-generation materials, battery manufacturing processes, and the impact of laser techniques on performance, safety, and scalability. The chapter concludes with insights into future prospects for laser applications in sustainable energy solutions.
entries.comment: 62 pages, 23 figures, preprint including the final bibliographic reference

entries.title: How Elasticity and Chiral Damping Shape Domain-Wall Creep
entries.abstract: Asymmetric domain-wall expansion in the creep regime provides an experimentally accessible probe of the interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (iDMI) and, in principle, chiral damping. However, severe discrepancies with complementary measurement techniques and the lack of a model describing the full experimental phenomenology of the creep of chiral domain walls, limits the application of these measurements. Here, using a symmetry decomposition of the velocity curve, we derive an analytical model describing the coupled influence of domain-wall stiffness and chiral damping in the creep regime. Their interplay generates the antisymmetric distortion that shifts the velocity minimum away from the DMI field. Applied to Co-based magnetic multilayers, the model yields iDMI values consistent with BLS and flow-regime benchmarks and identifies the reasons for the longstanding discrepancy. The model provides insights for possible strategies to measure chiral damping via creep dynamics of domain walls.
entries.comment: Main: 8 pages, 4 figures . Supplementary: 27 pages , 8 figures

entries.title: ThermoSight: From Appearance to Internal Thermofluid Fields via Physics-Guided Neural Reconstruction
entries.abstract: Most neural reconstruction methods focus on reproducing scene appearance, yet inferring physical states from visual observations is essential for machine understanding of the physical world. Reconstructing the internal temperature and soot fields of radiating thermofluids such as flames is challenging yet essential for improving energy efficiency and assessing heat exposure and fire spread. In flames, temperature and soot concentration jointly govern visible emission, and soot self-absorption alters the light that reaches each camera. With limited views, changes in the two fields can offset one another in the recorded RGB images, making temperature and soot difficult to disentangle. ThermoSight, a physics-guided neural framework for scientific imaging, jointly reconstructs continuous three-dimensional temperature and soot volume fraction fields from limited calibrated flame images without field-level ground truth during optimization. A differentiable spectral model links these fields to measured RGB through thermal emission, self-absorption, and calibrated camera responses. Temperature-dependent emission spectra and wavelength-dependent attenuation constrain shared fields across RGB channels, reducing temperature-soot ambiguity. Chromaticity consistency, observation-derived spatial constraints, and soot regularization complement intensity fitting. In a synthetic ablation, wavelength-resolved attenuation reduces temperature RMSE in the hot, sooty region from 234 to 112 K relative to a three-channel approximation, with nearly identical RGB PSNR (65.23 vs. 65.24 dB). Measured data yield coherent fields and competitive RGB reconstructions. These results demonstrate that physics-guided neural fields recover interpretable internal physical quantities beyond visually consistent appearance.

entries.title: Breaking the Fixed-Substrate Limitation of Deep Learning Ellipsometry with Pseudo-Substrate Spectra
entries.abstract: A machine learning method, deep learning ellipsometry (DLE), enables direct and rapid estimation of the optical constants and structures of thin films from spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) spectra. However, conventional neural-network-based DLE models are restricted to the specific substrate used during training, and applying them to a different substrate requires ~100 h of retraining. Here, we propose a framework that overcomes this fixed-substrate limitation by introducing a two-input feature-wise linear modulation DLE (FiLM-DLE). In this model, the SE spectra of a thin-film structure are input together with those of the substrate measured before film deposition, which we term the pseudo-substrate spectra. Any substrate, including a multilayer stack, is thus represented solely by its measured SE response, analogous to the pseudo-dielectric function, so that no prior knowledge of the substrate structure is required. Trained on a virtual dataset of 165 million samples representing metal, glass, and SiO2/Si substrates with different SiO2 thicknesses, a single FiLM-DLE model, trained once, extracts thin-film optical constants and structures with high accuracy and shows strong applicability to substrates not included in the training datasets. Experimental validation on 47 thin-film samples across diverse substrates yielded sample-averaged mean absolute errors, relative to conventional manual analysis, of 0.047 for refractive index, 0.030 for extinction coefficient, and 1.52 nm for thickness, with each analysis completed in under 2 s. FiLM-DLE thus eliminates the need for a separate DLE model for each substrate and enables rapid, high-accuracy optical characterization of thin films on diverse substrates.

entries.title: Polarization-Resilient Plasmonic Nanoantenna Arrays for Fiber-Coupled Terahertz Spectroscopy with Record-high Dynamic Range
entries.abstract: Achieving polarization-resilient optoelectronic responses while harnessing the strong light-matter interactions enabled by plasmonic nanostructures remains a fundamental challenge in ultrafast optoelectronics. Here, we demonstrate that the polarization sensitivity of plasmonic optoelectronic devices is governed not simply by optical absorption, but by its interplay with ultrafast photocarrier transport and local electric-field distributions, establishing a design principle for achieving polarization resilience without compromising optoelectronic efficiency. Through theoretical modeling and experimental validation, we demonstrate that this interplay enables plasmonic nanoantenna arrays to maintain highly efficient terahertz generation and detection across different optical polarization states, overcoming a longstanding limitation of plasmonic optoelectronics. Exploiting this principle, we introduce a high-power fiber-coupled terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) architecture that integrates polarization-resilient plasmonic nanoantenna arrays with hollow-core antiresonant fibers. By suppressing optical dispersion and nonlinearities during high-power femtosecond pulse delivery, this architecture unlocks the superior optoelectronic properties of GaAs-based photoconductors without sacrificing the flexibility and robustness of fiber coupling. The resulting system generates a record-high 2.1 mW of terahertz radiation and achieves a 145 dB peak dynamic range over 60 seconds, representing a 300-fold improvement over state-of-the-art fiber-coupled THz-TDS systems. This breakthrough opens new opportunities for probing weak light-matter interactions, characterizing strongly attenuating materials, and realizing high-throughput hyperspectral imaging and spatially distributed terahertz sensing beyond controlled laboratory environments.

entries.title: Broadband Absorption Bounds for Coated PEC Spheres: Curvature, Angular Momentum, and Localized Sources
entries.abstract: We investigate fundamental limits on broadband electromagnetic absorption by a material-coated perfectly electrically conducting (PEC) sphere. Exact reflection coefficients are derived for the transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) spherical modes. Their long-wavelength asymptotics, combined with causality and contour integration in the complex wavelength plane, yield sum rules relating the wavelength-integrated modal reflection to the static material parameters, coating thickness, curvature, and complex reflection zeros. For the dipolar modes (n=1), known passive spherical-wave sum rules establish analytically a material-dependent lower bound on the weighted logarithmic reflection integral. Extension to higher-order modes requires a nonnegativity condition on higher odd moments of the reflection zeros; we formulate this condition as a conjecture and provide extensive Monte-Carlo evidence for passive dispersive coatings. The resulting bounds establish a per-channel absorption–bandwidth tradeoff and reveal the spherical-harmonic order as a discrete transverse-wavenumber variable, recovering the familiar planar attenuation factor in the locally planar limit. Finally, we show how the modal bounds can be combined for a localized external source. For a radial electric dipole outside the sphere, the near-field excitation is decomposed into TM spherical channels, leading to a source-weighted broadband absorption bound. As the source approaches the surface, progressively higher angular momenta contribute, directly linking near-field spatial localization to the hierarchy of modal absorption constraints.

entries.title: Architectural Principles for Parameter-Efficient Unitary Transformations in Coherent Optical Neural Networks
entries.abstract: Coherent optical neural networks based on interferometric architectures offer a promising route toward high-throughput, energy-efficient computation by exploiting the multiple degrees of freedom of light, including spatial, temporal, and spectral modes. However, practical implementations are constrained by the number of tunable parameters due to fabrication complexity, device footprint, and control overhead. In such parameter-constrained settings, achieving high expressive power remains a central challenge. We identify two key architectural requirements for maintaining high expressive power under these constraints: (i) statistical uniformity in the implemented transformations and (ii) strong mixing capability per parameter, which enables rapid and unbiased redistribution of information across modes. To realize these requirements, we develop a logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology architecture whose fundamental building block is a single phase-shifter–beam-splitter pair, in contrast to conventional rectangular mesh architectures based on Mach-Zehnder interferometers. Computational evaluations show that, particularly at restricted parameter counts, the proposed architecture achieves lower matrix-reconstruction errors and higher classification accuracies than conventional meshes in both feedforward and recurrent networks. We further quantify these design principles using graph-theoretic measures, expected squared moduli of transformation-matrix entries, and matrix-reconstruction error. The resulting framework provides a quantitative and physically interpretable basis for parameter-efficient optical neural networks.

entries.title: Geometry-Derived Capacitance Dyadics with Floquet Sideband Correction for Anisotropic Periodic Patch Metasurfaces
entries.abstract: Homogenised sheet models describe periodic metallic patch layers using a scalar sheet capacitance, which is only valid when the effective response is isotropic. An isotropic response exists for unit cells with patch geometries that have rotational symmetry of order three or higher. Lower-symmetry unit cells with irregular or random geometries generically require a full 2 x 2 surface-capacitance dyadic. We present a framework that computes this dyadic directly from the arbitrary gap-connected patch geometry on a unit cell of a hexagonal lattice. The two-dimensional Bravais periodicity fixes the two independent macroscopic loading directions, the connectivity of the gap ensures a full-rank response for the geometries considered here, and the point-group symmetry of the patch constrains the form of the dyadic. A quasi-static boundary value problem on a single periodic cell then determines its independent entries. We use the surface-capacitance dyadic in the anisotropic surface- wave dispersion relation, which includes the leading spatially-dispersive first shell Floquet-sideband correction. For each new patch geometry, the dyadic and the first-shell correction are obtained from a single quasi-static cell problem and from the reconstructed boundary. So anisotropic surface- wave dispersion follows without a per-geometry full-wave eigenmode band sweep or sheet-tensor retrieval. We validate this geometry-to-dispersion chain against full-wave eigenmode simulations across six representative symmetry classes, showing that the correction captures band flattening near the Brillouin-zone boundary and improves agreement relative to the local dyadic model.

entries.title: Predicting local electric field in Al_xGa_(1-x)N p-i-n photodiodes using exciton Franz-Keldysh photocurrent spectroscopy
entries.abstract: In AlGaN p-i-n photodiodes, reverse bias redshifts and broadens the sub-bandgap photocurrent responsivity through the eXciton Franz-Keldysh (XFK) effect, and this spectral line shape encodes the local electric field inside the device. Fitting the photocurrent spectra of two such photodiodes, with 5% and 40% Al, to an XFK absorption model at each bias yields the local voltage, V_l, a single parameter that sets the line shape and uniquely determines the electric-field profile inside the device. In both devices, V_l varies linearly with the applied bias (R² = 0.994 and 0.998) but changes far more slowly than the bias itself, revealing a strong local reduction of the electric field that points to non-uniform electrostatics. The slopes show that only 12.4% of the applied bias in the 5% Al device, and 45.8% in the 40% Al device, drops across the junction at the probed location. Extrapolated to zero bias, V_l gives built-in voltages of 3.39 and 4.29 V, within 0.02 V of the 3.41 and 4.28 V obtained from technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulation, which validates the extracted local voltages at equilibrium. These results extend sub-bandgap photocurrent spectroscopy to AlGaN devices as an optical probe of local electrostatics, relevant to ultraviolet photodetectors and high-voltage electronics.

entries.title: Fourier-domain Crosstalk and Leakage Correction for Binary-Encoded Fourier Single-Pixel Imaging
entries.abstract: Digital micromirror devices enable high-speed Fourier single-pixel imaging (Fourier-SPI), but their binary modulation introduces quantization errors that degrade the reconstructed image quality. In particular, each binarized Fourier probe contains non-target Fourier components, thereby distorting the corresponding Fourier-domain measurement. This Letter presents a Fourier domain correction framework that characterizes these errors using the Fourier-domain response matrix of the decoded binary Fourier patterns. Accordingly, a response-matrix-based Fourier-SPI measurement model is established by partitioning the matrix into components associated with the sampled and unsampled frequencies, thereby decomposing the quantization error into sampled-frequency crosstalk and unsampled-frequency leakage. This model established a generalized correction framework, termed Fourier Crosstalk and Leakage Correction (FCLC), alongside two simplified methods: Fourier Sampled-Frequency Crosstalk Correction (FSCC) and Fourier DC Crosstalk Correction (FDCC). FSCC is implemented via an inversion-free Richardson-type iteration, whereas FDCC admits a closed-form solution. Numerical simulations and experiments across multiple binary encoding strategies reveal that the proposed framework improves reconstruction fidelity without modifying the binary patterns or acquisition process.

entries.title: Flat-band driven bipolar anomalous Nernst effect towards volt-scale transverse thermoelectric conversion
entries.abstract: Unipolar anomalous Nernst thermopiles are critically plagued by metallic interconnects, which induce heavy Joule dissipation and compromise the module's packing density, ultimately capping voltage generation. Here, we circumvent these limitations by establishing an intrinsic bipolar anomalous Nernst effect (BANE) paradigm, enabling seamless series integration analogous to Seebeck n-p pairs without passive metallic bridges. Focusing on flat-band topological systems, through machine learning assisted screening across multiple target properties, we identified 249 BANE materials, exhibiting near-room-temperature polarity switching. Guided by this predictive framework, we experimentally realized this phenomenon in single crystals of the Weyl ferromagnet, Co₂TiGe. Strikingly, while its intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) remains rigorously temperature-invariant up to the Curie temperature, the anomalous Nernst signal undergoes a sharp polarity inversion across T ≈225 K. First-principles calculations attribute this behavior to the interplay between flat bands and Weyl nodes, where thermal depopulation shifts the chemical potential across the band edge, inverting the sign of ∂σ_(xy) / ∂ε via the Mott relation. This work opens an avenue toward compact, monolithic transverse thermopiles capable of volt-scale generation free from interfacial parasitic dissipation.

entries.title: Tunable Multi-Frequency-Band Generator and Detector of AC Signals Based on a Spin Hall Device with Two Antiferromagnetic Layers
entries.abstract: Antiferromagnetic (AFM) spin Hall oscillators offer an electrical route to compact terahertz sources, while AFM spin Hall diodes can be used as a promising detectors of terahertz signals, however, their attainable frequency and the redout efficiency are constrained by the dynamics of a single AFM layer. We theoretically and numerically investigate a spin Hall multilayer junction Pt/AFM/Pt/AFM/Pt comprising two canted AFM layers, driven by independent drive DC currents flowing in the outer platinum (Pt) layers. Using a model based on the coupled Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert-Slonczewski equations for four AFM sublattices and a phase-dependent two-interface spin Hall magnetoresistance model, we show that the device manifests itself as a DC current-driven oscillating spin Hall magnetoresistance. When an additional DC (AC) signal current is applied to the junction, the device generates an output AC (DC) voltage. Our model predicts current-driven, locked, co- and counter-rotational states of the net magnetization at Neel-vector frequencies in the top and bottom AFM layers, respectively. These states result in a multi-frequency response of the spin Hall magnetoresistance at the sum and difference frequencies. The counter-rotation regime additionally activates the phase-sensitive mixing contribution, producing a fourth harmonic. In contrast, the co-rotation regime provides a difference-frequency channel on the order of 100 GHz, although mutual locking prevents this output from being tuned continuously toward zero. Our estimations show that the device matched to an external load can generate output AC power of 1.2 nW at the second harmonic and 0.8 pW at the fourth harmonic, and can produce a DC voltage of about 1 mV for a 6 mA input signal current.

entries.title: Reflective Spin Wave Filtering Limiters with Bandpass to Bandstop Bifurcation
entries.abstract: Spin wave (SW) filters using thin-film yttrium iron garnet are an attractive technology for reconfigurable and software defined radio (SDR) systems in which parameters such as channel frequency or transmit power are adjusted in real time to efficiently utilize constrained spectrum resources. Operating in congested electromagnetic environments leave communication systems vulnerable to damage or disruption from strong interference and jamming. Therefore, frequency tunable filters and power limiters are needed to support SDR operation on the physical layer. Here, we report a frequency tunable bandpass filtering limiter which reflects excess above threshold power using a network of nonlinear SW resonators in a ladder filter topology. The reported devices show insertion losses as low as 3.29 dB, isolation above 14.22 dB, center frequency tuning over more than two octaves from 4.75 GHz to 21.08 GHz, fast transient response of 14.01 ns, and low transient spike leakage. A physics-informed nonlinear SW model is discussed and a method to simulate and design networks of nonlinear resonators is introduced.
